speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Vikram Nair, you may wish to take both cuts together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In 2017, the geopolitical landscape continued to evolve rapidly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China’s strategic and economic clout remains on an upward trend.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Members would have noted China playing a more active and assertive role in global affairs in recent years.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: China is clearly becoming an outward-looking global power, ready to play a bigger role in the world and many countries hungry for investments appreciate this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, observers have juxtaposed China's rising prominence on the international stage against perceptions of the declining United States (US) influence in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Closer to home, unresolved tensions persist on the Korean Peninsula.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Around the world, other national and international challenges abound.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Countries are grappling with transnational terrorism, sluggish economies and structural challenges of demographics and integration, and the worrying trend of growing nationalist sentiment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The growing threat of terrorism has been spurred by the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS), which has been fighting primarily in Iraq and Syria.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They have mastered the art of using social media to radicalise individuals.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The wars themselves have caused record numbers of refugees to flow outwards, including to places like Europe.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This, in turn, has led the local politics in these countries to become increasingly nationalistic and unfriendly to immigrants and refugees, often characterising them not only as economic threats but also as potential breeding grounds for terrorists.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has led to the growth and popularity of far-right movements in many developed countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another hallmark of our times is the development and democratisation of technology that would have been unthinkable just a few decades ago.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, individuals, companies and governments have almost all their private information in digital form, making it potentially easy to access such information, both legally and illegally, by hacking and gaining access to existing databases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We are not yet fully cognisant of the effects that technologies, such as digital media, will have on us and our societies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: How can Singapore continue to navigate and protect our interests in an increasingly complex and uncertain geopolitical environment?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has traditionally been an important participant in regional agreements and partnerships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These include both formal frameworks, such as the founding of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and their other related work as well as dialogues to bring together important partners.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our Shangri-La Dialogue for Defence is one good example of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Recently, there have been media reports on the revival of the "Quadrilateral Security Dialogue" among the US, Japan, India and Australia to deepen security cooperation and to coordinate alternatives for regional integration.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These four countries are good friends of ours and have a shared commitment to the existing "rules-based order" as a key mechanism for protecting and projecting their own principal security and economic interests.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It seems like it would be helpful for Singapore and, potentially ASEAN, to engage and support such initiatives.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: What is MFA's view of how Singapore and ASEAN will be affected by such regional initiatives?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, the shift in global economic weight to Asia was highlighted in the Budget Statement this year.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We witness the opening up of China as an awakening of an economic giant.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: But China would also face a severely ageing society and rising labour costs over time.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In these respects, if it could maintain political stability, India may have the advantages and better growth prospects in the longer term.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: This shift in global economic weight to Asia poses new diplomatic challenges for us, especially when the US is going through a relatively incoherent phase in its engagement with Asia because of domestic politics.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is not caught between a rock and hard place, but among three powers, namely, China, India and the US, while deeply embedded in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The South China Sea threatens to become the great game for the powers.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The prime example is India's strengthening military and economic ties with Vietnam, which include an oil concession in disputed waters of the South China Sea and the warming of US-Vietnam ties in an effort to counterbalance China.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: ASEAN seems divided and the countries distracted by domestic strife, with ethnic conflicts becoming a major issue for the grouping, Myanmar is an example.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: We also have strong ties with China, India and the US.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: As ASEAN Chair, how can we bring these deep and strong ties to help maintain the balance of power in Asia?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: With our experience in fostering grassroots multiracialism, what can we do to build deeper ties to the peoples of Southeast Asia and bring diverse communities closer together to build a more resilient ASEAN?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Chairman, many of us in Singapore watch with bated breath as the United Kingdom (UK) voted on the Referendum on its European Union (EU) membership and, more recently, when the US voted for its 45th President.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These were divisive campaigns marked by catchy populist slogans and contagious promises.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The results showed a deep frustration with the status quo and anxiety about the future in a globalised world marked by free trade.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore thrives on an open economy, and trade is our lifeblood.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given these developments, what is MFA's view on the prospects for free trade and economic integration around the world?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Further, Singapore takes over the chairmanship of ASEAN this year and will strive to deepen regional connectivity.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With this year's theme of resilience and innovation, efforts will be underway to uphold the regional order to better deal with emerging security challenges, tap new ways to manage and mine digital technologies and push ahead with regional economic integration.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Growth in developed markets is slowing while protectionist sentiments appear to be on the rise.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In this regard, one of Singapore's strategies is to continue diversifying our international connections.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a growing number of emerging economies that are attracting global interest and offering opportunities for our businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore should consider how to strengthen our partnership with these countries.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Looking beyond our traditional markets like Southeast Asia and China, I would like to highlight four regions of emerging markets with economic potential.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Could we have an update on Singapore's engagement with Europe and Euro-Asia?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There have been several high-level visits to Latin America in recent years, including then President Tony Tan's State Visit to Mexico in 2016, which was the first by a Singaporean Head of State to the region.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In view of the increase in high-level exchanges with Latin America, how has our relationship with the region's two main trade blocs, the Pacific Alliance and Mercosur, progressed?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am sure it will provide opportunities for us to further strengthen economic cooperation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In sub-Saharan Africa, notwithstanding its challenges, the countries continue to embark on a path of development and urbanisation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This presents us with opportunities in areas where we have expertise, such as urban solutions, water, waste management, energy and logistics.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What further steps are being taken to broaden and deepen Singapore's engagement of these emerging markets and what more can be done to open up new economic opportunities there?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: At that time, during the Cold War, ASEAN was an important alliance where countries were largely aligned on political matters and sought to foster cooperation and economic growth together.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: When the Cold War ended, ASEAN grew and welcomed more countries into the alliance, focused on economic growth and cooperation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This was the era that Francis Fukuyama described as being the "End of History", by which he meant the end of historic contests of ideologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In recent years, though, ASEAN's plans have grown and there have been plans for greater economic integration, including a common market for goods and services.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: At the same time, differences have emerged among members on certain issues, such as the South China Sea, making it difficult for them to reach consensus.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: In 2018, Singapore will take the reins of the ASEAN Chairmanship.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This is an important opportunity for Singapore to exercise leadership and contribute to ASEAN's role in the region.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What are our priorities for our year as Chairman?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What can ASEAN do to remain forward-looking to chart a better future for the region?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What will ASEAN do to get through both its internal and external challenges, and what can we, as Chair of ASEAN, do to help foster consensus on these difficult issues?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Our aim is to connect people and economies seamlessly across the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: It is also critical to lead the way in keeping the economic integration vibrant and the region competitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: The Minister for Foreign Affairs said, "We gain more by working together".

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Several initiatives are in the framework and I would like to highlight three.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One, the formation of a network of ASEAN Smart Cities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Here, boosting cybersecurity is also in the pipeline and on the agenda.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Can we have details, sustainable goals as well as timelines for some of these proposed initiatives and what are some of the challenges we can expect to face?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, knowing that ASEAN comprises nations in various stages of development, modernisation and urbanisation, the harmonisation and alignment, as well as contributions, will have differences and will surface discrepancies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, Sir, ASEAN commemorated its 50th anniversary last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As a pioneer founder of ASEAN and as a respected and constructive diplomatic stakeholder, it is apposite that Singapore finds itself as the first Chair of ASEAN after the celebration of its golden jubilee in 2017.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is apposite because Singapore is seen as an important thought leader, both within and outside ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has the potential to shape and determine the substance of the discussions that take precedence among our regional partners because of our reputation as an honest broker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has chosen the themes of resilience and innovation as its Chairmanship tagline with a view to building a future-ready ASEAN which is adaptable and forward-looking.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of such a treaty is potentially an important development in addressing some of Singapore’s bilateral flashpoints that have reared their ugly head in the past, at times, with certain political leaders in Indonesia.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such an extradition treaty could inject a newfound trust and confidence into the Singapore-Indonesia relationship which, like ASEAN, also celebrated its golden jubilee last year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Last year, Singapore announced that it was focusing on steps to enhance e-commerce through its National Trade Platform, a one-stop trade information platform for customs clearance, trade logistics and trade finance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Alongside this specific initiative, it would also appear that the prospect of the ASEAN Single Window would allow local Singaporean businesses to connect to more customers throughout ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, all foreign policy begins at home and I request some information from the Minister on the roles the Ministry plays from a whole-of-Government perspective in translating foreign policy initiatives into economic outcomes for enterprises in Singapore in view of our economic transformation plans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, one of ASEAN’s interests in COC is to ensure that trade and freedom of movement of sea traffic, particularly commercial traffic, is unimpeded.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would appear that China’s interests in the South China Sea are territorial to the extent that it wants a high degree of control of its immediate backyard, behaviour which does not appear to be primarily driven by a desire to bully ASEAN, but rather is consistent with modern big power behaviour in regions adjacent to its immediate borders, regardless of whether such a power is an Anglo-Saxon one or not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What more can Singapore do to smooth over the concerns China has about the South China Sea and secure a stable future between ASEAN and China going forward?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The AEC Blueprint 2025 was also adopted by ASEAN leaders to provide broad directions to guide the next phase of economic integration from 2016 to 2025.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: The business community and our people also do not understand the benefits of AEC.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In order to help our local businesses to seize business opportunities in AEC, it would be useful if MFA and the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) can organise more industry-focused talks and forums.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Such meetings will also provide opportunities for our business leaders to forge partnerships with other ASEAN business leaders.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Instead of just focusing on our business leaders, we can extend this programme to other business leaders in ASEAN.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this way, more opportunities can be created for our business leaders to forge partnerships.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Second, an update on the AEC’s progress and achievements to date.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, separate surveys completed by researchers in a university and a private polling firm indicate that Singaporeans have greater ambivalence, less interest and less sense of belonging towards ASEAN, compared to our ASEAN partners.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is indifference and even scepticism towards ASEAN, even though there is some acknowledgement that the grouping benefits Singapore in terms of economic opportunities and regional stability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I find these results not satisfactory, since our future is inextricably linked to the success of ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given that these views are about how Singapore relates to and interacts with our closest neighbours – countries with which Singapore has to work with closely with on various issues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder if such sentiments and ignorance might harm Singapore in the longer term.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister if he intends to do anything to promote more positive views of ASEAN among Singaporeans, especially given the fact that Singapore is serving as ASEAN Chair this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the Minister wishes to pursue such action, I would like to invite him to explain what these initiatives are.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would also appreciate the Minister informing this House about how he expects such plans to continue past Singapore’s chairing of ASEAN, and how they relate to the ASEAN Social Cultural Community.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Terrorists have also used this issue to recruit more people, including those in Malaysia, to join their cause.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, all ASEAN states have expressed a deep commitment to the importance of human rights, for example, Article 14 of the ASEAN Charter, which forms the basis of the ASEAN Intergovernmental Commission on Human Rights (AICHR), the ASEAN Commission on the Promotion and Protection of the Rights of Women and Children (ACWC), and the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ASEAN has concertedly alleviated humanitarian situations previously, for example, the earthquake in Aceh in December 2016.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I would like to ask: one, what can ASEAN do in response to this humanitarian crisis?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, how can the ASEAN Human Rights Declaration, ASEAN Charter and other ASEAN legal agreements form a stronger basis for engaging Myanmar to take greater humanitarian action?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And three, as ASEAN Chair, what can Singapore do to alleviate the humanitarian situation?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Amrin Amin, you can take both cuts.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Mr Chairman, China's growth has been impressive since the country opened up to the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: It is expected to register 6.4% growth in 2018.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: China’s growth, affluence and rising middle class represent opportunities for Singaporeans and Singaporean firms.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Already, many Singapore companies are invested in China.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has always strongly believed in China’s growth prospects.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Last year, Singapore and China agreed to work together on the B&R Initiative.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: China's prosperity and growth have brought about greater confidence among the people of China about their country.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: China is widely seen as a rising power and becoming more prominent in the international arena.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Given our stake in China's growth, Singaporeans have an interest in our engagement with China and the state of our bilateral relationship.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Could MFA provide an update on the Singapore-China relationship?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: A key force shaping the geopolitical environment is US-China relations.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: China's rise has fuelled speculations of a fundamental change in world order.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Projects like the B&R Initiative signal China's increasing global influence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Such trends have contributed to a broader concern of a tussle between the US and China in the near future, as both sides may jostle for strategic space and influence.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: For Singapore, both the US and China are important partners.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: We have close cooperation with both countries, extensive trade and investment links and many people-to-people exchanges.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: Given the brewing rhetoric of a strategic rivalry between the US and China and in view of our good relations with both the US and China, we have a stake in ensuring good, stable US-China relations.

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: What is MFA's view on the state of US-China relations?

speaker: Mr Amrin Amin (Sembawang)
text: As both countries are strategically important for Singapore, how will Singapore be affected by any fluctuations in US-China relations and how can we mitigate such an impact?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore and the US enjoy strong, multifaceted and long-standing relations, spanning the defence, economic and security fields.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Defence ties are excellent, with both sides working together in the area of counterterrorism.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The Prime Minister's visit to Washington DC in October last year at the invitation of President Donald Trump reaffirmed the mutually beneficial nature of the bilateral relationship.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: However, in the past year, we have also witnessed the US' withdrawal from TPP as well as the Paris Agreement on Climate Change, amongst other developments.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These actions have led some to question the US' commitment to the rules-based global order that it has underwritten since World War II, and the effects that this could have on Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, can the Minister provide an update on the state of Singapore-US relations and how Singapore has been working with the US to ensure that bilateral relations remain stable?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Aside from direct air links to all three countries, we share land borders with Malaysia, and maritime boundaries with Malaysia and Indonesia.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: We have large amounts of trade and investments flowing between us and our neighbours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: The people of our countries share long-standing historical and familial ties.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: With Brunei, we share a close friendship, one which both sides have often described as a "special relationship".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: There has been much progress in bilateral cooperation between Singapore and our three neighbours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: There are more companies investing in Indonesia than before.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Our youth exchanges with Brunei continue to grow.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: As with all neighbours, we sometimes have differences, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: I note that Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak has just participated in the 8th Singapore-Malaysia Leaders' Retreat in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Minister for Foreign Affairs Dr Vivian Balakrishnan also recently visited Jakarta, where he met several political officeholders and politicians.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, Deputy Prime Minister Teo Chee Hean visited Brunei last year, where I was a delegation member.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: First, would MFA be able to update Members of the House on the state of our bilateral relations with our three closest neighbours, including key takeaways from the recent visits?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: How will we work to maintain our relations with our closest neighbours for the benefit of our peoples?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Second, as Malaysia enters into election mode, what is MFA's view on its impact on bilateral relations, if any?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Third, following the commemoration of our 50th anniversary of formal diplomatic relations with Indonesia last year, what are some of the bilateral projects that we can look forward to that will help to strengthen our relationship with Indonesia and maintain the positive momentum of bilateral ties?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Mr Chairman, my cut is on Singapore's relations with Japan and the Republic of Korea and how we can improve cooperation with these countries for mutual benefit.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singapore has excellent relations with Japan and Korea.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: However, such good state of affairs needs to be nurtured continually.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Over the past year, I would like to ask the Minister whether there have been high level exchanges for both Japan and Korea.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Additionally, were there also business-to-business and people-to-people exchanges between Japan and Korea on the one hand, and Singapore on the other?

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Many Japanese and Korean companies have also made investments and set up offices in Singapore to tap the growing Southeast Asia market.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Singapore is also host to many Japanese and Koreans living, working and schooling here.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Similarly, some Singaporeans are also drawn to study and work in Japan and Korea, embracing their culture and bringing back with them many valuable experiences.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: For example, both Japan and Singapore are experiencing ageing societies.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: I think there are many lessons we can learn from each other.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Both Korea and Japan are also technologically advanced countries.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng (Pioneer)
text: Is Singapore looking into avenues where these companies can partner our local enterprises, especially our small and medium enterprises (SMEs), to access their respective markets and even to partner with to access third countries' markets?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I understand that Australia and Singapore enjoy a strong relationship.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This strong relationship is exemplified by substantive cooperation at the government-to-government level, as well as at international forums, including those involving ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides the frequent exchange of high-level visits, we also have the Singapore-Australia Joint Ministerial Committee, a unique dialogue mechanism involving foreign affairs, defence and trade ministers, which has been going on for two decades now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Over the years, Australia has generously allotted space for our Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) soldiers to train.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This, alongside a history of co-deployment and operational cooperation, is a testament to the high level of trust between our two countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On top of that, our people-to-people ties are healthy.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Australians readily reciprocate this, with over one million of them visiting Singapore every year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With these in mind, I invite the Minister for Foreign Affairs to update the House on Singapore's relations with Australia, as well as the ongoing implementation of the 10-year CSP, which is in its third year.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This was exemplified in January 2018 at the ASEAN-India Commemorative Summit where the ASEAN countries and India reaffirmed their commitment to strong ASEAN-India ties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is happening in tandem with the shift in the global economic weight towards Asia that the Minister for Finance mentioned in his Budget Statement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With its economic growth, India has become an increasingly important power on the world stage.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A growing India represents significant opportunities for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek an update from MFA on the state of our relations with India.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef, you can take both cuts together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Change seems to be ongoing all the time, including the geopolitical and humanitarian issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Not surprisingly, some of our businesses and entrepreneurs view the region through a more guarded perspective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Despite all these, there is still movement into the region, and some new markets have taken shape.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How will our engagement with the Middle East progress and proceed?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: What are the current emerging markets that we are exploring and with the view towards our economic expansion in the Middle East?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: These will, of course, be dependent on our diplomatic ties with the region.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Thus, how does the Minister foresee us moving forward here?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: The last year has seen the Middle East issue taking centrestage yet again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: Ongoing issues persist and new conflicts, too, have surfaced.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: One of the long-term controversial matters is the Israeli-Palestinian issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: With an understanding of the changes that have evolved, how will we continue to uphold our principle?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: How do we also continue to engage both sides in the long-drawn conflict, moving forward?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef
text: What about our relations with the other countries in the area, such as the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kuwait and Oman?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Mr Chairman, the geopolitical situation has gone through significant changes over the past few years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Europe, by and large, has remained a source of stability.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This has created a stable environment for us to further our long-standing relations and good economic ties with Europe.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Can I ask MFA: how are we strengthening our relations with our European partners and with the EU as a whole?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond economic cooperation, how can we deepen our cooperation with our European partners in other areas, such as connectivity?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I note that there has been an increased interest in developments in the Arctic, and these are well-covered by the media.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Major countries have also recently made important announcements regarding their Arctic plans.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: How will Singapore respond to the opportunities and potential challenges for Europe, including the Arctic?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, in the various overseas work trip I have been to, I have witnessed the calibre and dedication of our ambassadors, our non-resident ambassadors and our MFA officers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Their hard work has continued to advance the interests of our country, and I would like to offer them my sincere appreciation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And these issues are often worsened by climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I saw little children's childhood shattered; I saw young people all alone, having watched their family members get killed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: All these issues are complex and interlinked, requiring resolute political will by the international community to work together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore has always been a strong supporter of multilateral approaches to global issues.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How is Singapore working at the ASEAN level, particularly as the current Chair, as well as at the international level, to address challenges, such as climate change and the Rohingya refugee crisis?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore has, historically, positioned itself as a centre for global exchange and a key hub for trade and investment.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We are now one of the world's most highly connected cities and are exposed to and facilitate massive flows of data and information with other cultures and economies.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: To remain relevant and competitive, we fight and compete for ideas, opinions and talent in the global marketplace.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In this matrix, therefore, it is inevitable that we become susceptible to external influences.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Consequentially, Singapore will now not only need to rally support for its foreign policy positions with our international partners, such as our ASEAN neighbours, but also domestically amongst us Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Over the past year, there had been several instances that reflect this.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The South China Sea dispute has been widely reported in the mass media and commented upon in governmental and academic circles.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A territorial dispute between some of our ASEAN neighbours and China alludes to a larger geopolitical strategic tussle for global influence between the dominant global superpower, that is, the US, and a rising China.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The situation in the Rakhine state in Myanmar is another potentially divisive issue within ASEAN.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are divergent views on this complex intercommunal issue among ASEAN member states, and it could undermine ASEAN unity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Based on this backdrop of recent incidents and events, it is clear that within consensus-based ASEAN, there are members with strong divergent views, both within ASEAN and with our dialogue partners.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: ASEAN will not only have to navigate fishes amongst its member states but also with external actors.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As such, the diverse and sometimes contrasting interests of different ASEAN members and other external influences could cause various actors who may seek to influence Singapore, as ASEAN Chair, in order to get their way on the regional platform.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I invite the Minister to share with us on how we can, as a country, respond to these possible external challenges and influences.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Singapore is a small country located in Southeast Asia, one of the most diverse regions in the world.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Maintaining strong political, economic and people-to-people ties with other countries in our region is essential.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: But as the Chinese saying goes, 远亲不如近邻, while the majority of Singaporean forefathers came from China, it is equally, if not more important, for Singapore to build and maintain strong relations with the countries in our immediate Southeast Asian region.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Among the ASEAN members, given the proximity in terms of geography, language and culture, there is natural familiarity of Singapore and Singaporeans with our immediate neighbours: Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: However, let us also not forget or neglect our other neighbours.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, I have observed first-hand, as part of the Prime Minister's delegation to Vietnam in March 2017, and then-Speaker Mdm Halimah Yacob's delegation to Laos in September 2014, how we build upon our multifaceted ties and complementarities to strengthen mutual understanding and cooperation.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: In this context, I would like an update from MFA on Singapore’s engagement of our fellow ASEAN countries, in particular, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, on resources for MFA, geopolitical developments happen around the clock and are often unpredictable in nature.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Our civil servants from MFA have the unenviable task of regularly monitoring global geopolitics 24/7 so as to provide timely and well-considered responses.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: MFA officers will have to react round-the-clock to develop and coordinate well with fellow ASEAN member states and key partners, as well as across the entire Singapore Government, in order to ensure a successful chairmanship.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: This is important so that Singapore's chairmanship can produce progress in regional cooperation that benefits Singapore and also other ASEAN states.

speaker: Mr Cedric Foo Chee Keng
text: Given the demands placed on MFA, particularly this year, does MFA have the necessary resources to carry out its work with adroitness and sensitivity, as they always have?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, Singapore's Foreign Service Officers play important roles in defending Singapore's interest in the global arena, be it representing Singapore at multilateral meetings, responding to international crises or rendering consular assistance to Singaporeans in distress overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Given the increasing demands on MFA's work, there is a need for MFA to ensure that it has sufficient manpower and competencies to meet these challenges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How will MFA ensure that its officers are equipped with the necessary training, knowledge and capabilities to fulfil its mission?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Has MFA also explored tapping on mid-career applicants for these posts and, if so, what percentage of its Foreign Service Officers are made up of mid-career entrants?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How can MFA also work with overseas Singaporeans and agencies, such as Enterprise Singapore, to enhance its capabilities?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, given our fundamental realities as a small country and an open economy dependent on global trade, Singapore is exposed to the headwinds of global developments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When we watch videos or read accounts of events that take place far from Singapore, it does not matter that they may be happening thousands of miles away.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They have an effect on us intellectually, as well as emotionally, and shape our views on how Singapore should conduct itself on the international stage.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, social media has led to a greater proliferation and contestation of narratives in the marketplace of ideas, with fake news being a growing and very real threat.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given these developments, it has become even more important for the Government to communicate clearly to Singaporeans to foster greater awareness and understanding of the foreign policy stance that Singapore takes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are the key principles that Singaporeans should know on Singapore's foreign policy?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a multi-ethnic and religious country, how concerned should Singaporeans be that foreign policy issues may be dragged into the domestic discourse?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Ministry share with the man-in-the-street what it means for Singapore to be ASEAN Chair?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What are its significance and impact on us as a nation?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chairman, as a country whose only resource is its people, Singapore believes that human resource (HR) development is vital for economic and social progress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore benefited from technical assistance provided by other countries and international organisations in our early post-Independence years.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How has SCP supported our engagement of other countries?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Mr Chairman, Singaporeans are going overseas to live, study and work in increasing numbers.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of them have become prominent leaders in their chosen fields.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite spending many years abroad, there is a large number of such Singaporeans who continue to maintain ties with families and friends here.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They remain spiritually rooted in Singapore and are proud to be Singaporeans and not just because they missed the local hawker food.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In many ways, they are also the face of Singapore to those with whom they interact in their new countries.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They are also often called upon to explain and, sometimes, to defend Singapore's policies and actions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Given their unique position of being Singaporeans immersed in another society and culture, is there a role for overseas Singaporeans to advocate for Singapore, presenting our point of view to the rest of the world?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: If we believe that this can be a significant source of soft power for Singapore, I would like to ask the Minister what can we do to help them in their role.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many Singaporeans work and study overseas and based in foreign lands for many months and even years.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Many also make short business trips and holidays.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: When we are abroad, we are largely on our own and would have to be alert and careful.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: But despite our best plans, our overseas trips can often be thwarted by unforeseen circumstances that could range from natural disasters to terror attacks.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: These are beyond the control of any of us and it can create stress for Singaporeans overseas and even pose dangers to their lives.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The affected Singaporeans would then require assistance and support, and their families and friends back home will also be concerned with their status and well-being.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: We do not need to look far for past examples.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Terrorist attacks in European countries, as well as unrest in other parts of the world, will require Singaporeans to be ever vigilant when abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chairman, now, to discuss my day job in MFA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I want to thank all the Members for your very insightful contributions and comments.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I want to commend Mr Low Thia Khiang, Ms Sylvia Lim and Mr Pritam Singh for your also very constructive comments.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, I listened to you very carefully and I could not find anything to disagree with you.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And I am sure our foreign partners will notice that there is bipartisan support for our approach to foreign policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Indeed, as a small open state, we need the bipartisan support.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, I am grateful for your constructive contributions and for the bipartisan support that we enjoy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There are at least three key political issues, if I could summarise.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The third political issue is that Singapore is an open multiracial, multi-religious city-state, a sovereign country in the heart of Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And yet, as Mr Low Thia Khiang mentioned yesterday, this cultural arbitrage is also Singapore's competitive advantage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we need to be aware of all the opportunities as well as the challenges that confront us because of our unique position.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In his Budget Statement, the Minister for Finance identified three major transformations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: A shift in the global centre of gravity towards Asia, and that, basically, as Mr Low says, is China, India and ASEAN itself.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, the emergence of new technologies and the impact it will have on jobs, the economy and even attitudes to free trade.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The ageing population is especially an issue that confronts Singapore and China, and the fact that, in contrast, for ASEAN as a whole, 60% of ASEAN is below the age of 35.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These three trends present us with both opportunities and threats.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What we are trying to do is that as Asia grows, to make use of our unique identity, unique position and even our unique cultural arbitrage in order to ride on our region's growth and dynamism.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But even as we do this, we must also be mindful that there are multiple transboundary pitfalls.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For instance, protectionist nationalism is on the rise.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the midst of the digital revolution, cybersecurity breaches and “fake news” have eroded trust in institutions and divided societies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, sometimes, they have even become a tool of foreign policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First, Singapore has to be successful and vibrant.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If we are not successful, we are not relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As Minister Mentor Lee Kuan Yew said a long time ago, the world will not miss us if we disappear as a small state.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There is no irreplaceable function that a small state provides the rest of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second, we must preserve our ability to make independent sovereign decisions based on our own national interests, and we must not become a vassal state.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are not for sale and we are not going to be easily intimidated.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Third, Singapore aims to be a friend to all.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: What this means is that we do not wish to be forced to choose sides, nor to be caught in proxy battles.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Fourth, we promote and we believe in a global rules-based order with international law and international norms.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If you think about it, this is essential precisely because we are a small state.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Fifth, we must be a reliable, credible and consistent partner.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For us, we do not have the luxury of changing, flip-flopping, changing our views quickly over time, or saying different things to different partners.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We need to be reliable, credible and consistent.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I will start by addressing our relationships with the major powers.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Amrin Amin asked about our relationship with China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Many Members have also asked about US-China relations and their dynamics, and how that affects us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: With China, our relations, our track record of cooperation are deep, long-standing and substantive.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Last September, Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong visited Beijing at China’s invitation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The timing was significant because it was just a couple of weeks before China's 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We did not expect that they would have the bandwidth; nevertheless, they invited the Prime Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I am quoting him and we will convey the exact words in Chinese words to the media later on.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, this is our own long-standing belief.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have always believed that a successful China, a stable China, is good for our region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The rise of China and the elevation of hundreds of millions of people from abject poverty to middle class is the biggest story of our lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And, as Mr Low Thia Khiang said yesterday, as people with Chinese ancestry at a cultural level and emotional level, we must take pride and joy in that achievement.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we are also aware that we are not Chinese citizens and Singapore is the only political entity, the only state in the world, where Chinese are a majority, but we are not under the Communist Party of China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have always consistently supported China's strategic economic development.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is clearly evident from our unique government-to-government projects: Suzhou Industrial Park, Tianjin Eco-city and, more recently, the Chongqing Demonstration Initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Of course, our role will have to evolve because, unlike the past two-and-a-half decades when we were investing and we were moving concepts and ideas into China, today, China has become a net exporter of capital and technology.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, our role inevitably must evolve to keep up with the times.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The other point that we must anticipate and must expect from time to time is that there will be issues of differences between Singapore and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: After all, we are two sovereign states with very different national circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we must expect differences in perspectives and we must not get flustered even when pressured.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is almost par for the course in international relations because you cannot expect two countries’ interests to be completely identical.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I mean we have had some bumps along the way, but I would say these episodes over the last two-and-a-half years have helped both sides to understand each other’s position better.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think it has made for a more mature relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This will further enhance market access for our companies and create more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Of course, we also want to see more Chinese companies accessing opportunities in Southeast Asia through Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Both sides have identified new areas for cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have the Joint Council for Bilateral Cooperation (JCBC), co-led by Deputy Prime Minister Teo.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have now identified finance, legal and judicial sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: One example was the inaugural Singapore-China Legal and Judicial Roundtable held last year.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These initiatives will complement the existing high-level fora on economic cooperation, social governance and leadership.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: All, again, are incidentally chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Teo.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These extensive and high-level engagements between China and Singapore epitomise the long track record that builds trust and confidence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The B&R Initiative is another major opportunity of cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When I visited China in June last year, Foreign Minister Wang Yi and I agreed to establish three platforms to deepen B&R cooperation: first, on infrastructural connectivity; second, on financial connectivity and support; and third, to look for opportunities for third-party collaboration, including joint training for officials from other B&R countries to work and to exploit opportunities that the B&R Initiative provides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And nearly one-third of China's outbound investments to B&R countries actually flow through Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I double-checked with my staff and they said yes, these figures are from China itself.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are working together to connect the overland Silk Road Economic Belt with the Maritime Silk Road through a new "Southern Transport Corridor" which links Chongqing in western China, to Beibu Gulf in Guangxi.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our businesses can expand into western China through Chongqing, just as Chinese companies can use Singapore as a gateway into Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This creates a "mutual hub effect", which benefits businesses and people.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And, as I said, by interconnecting the overland Silk Road with the Maritime Silk Road, it still maintains Singapore as a hub.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US is a long-standing, close strategic partner.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have had mutually beneficial relations over the last 52 years.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Defence ties form the backbone of the bilateral relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When Hurricane Harvey struck last year, we quickly deployed four Republic of Singapore Air Force (RSAF) CH-47 Chinook helicopters and 34 of our own servicemen from a training detachment in Grand Prairie, Texas, to help with the relief efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: RSAF was able to work seamlessly with their American counterparts because of the regular training between both sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have 1,000 SAF servicemen training in various detachments in Arizona, Idaho and Texas on the F15s, F16s, Chinooks and Apaches.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: No other foreign state has more troops on US soil.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our strong trade, investment and business ties with the US are underpinned by the 2004 US-Singapore FTA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US is Singapore's largest trading partner in services and the third largest trading partner in goods.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our total trade with the US stood at almost S$140 billion.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There are over 4,200 US companies here, which help create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is a statistic we shared with President Trump to make the point that he has real skin in the game in Southeast Asia and, especially in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore is the second largest Asian investor in the US, second after Japan, and Asia’s No 1 buyer of US commercial property.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Last month’s Singapore Airshow showcased our strong defence and economic cooperation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US fielded the largest foreign delegation with 170 exhibitors.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: US aerospace exports to Singapore totalled almost US$5 billion in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: These deep economic linkages have given Singapore access to US markets and US technology and allowed Singaporeans to learn with and from the best in the US, including the academic and research institutes.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Prime Minister Lee's visit to Washington last October reinforced these fundamentals.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: President Trump described Singapore as one of the US’ “closest strategic partners in Asia”.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There have been questions about the US' commitment to the liberal world order and free trade as we know it.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: One statistic which I think Members of the House should be aware of is that, in 1960, the US GDP was 40% of global GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The reason for giving Members these statistics is to make you all appreciate that it is a completely legitimate political exercise within domestic US politics to ask why they should unilaterally underwrite the global world order as we have known it for the past 70 years when their share is shrinking.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I say this because you need to look for deeper trends beyond the headlines and the personalities.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But the point we make is that the US has had a headstart here.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The US has enormous investments in Southeast Asia; the US has significant reservoirs of goodwill.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is theirs to lose, even as they sort out their domestic political questions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We want, and, in fact, are well-suited to be part of the common circle of friends.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Remember my earlier point about not being forced to choose sides.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we must anticipate that there will be an element of competition between the US and China.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But the big difference from, say, the Cold War, is that the US and China are highly interdependent in a way which was never present in the relationship between the Soviet Union and the US.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, we hope that both sides will see that there is too much to lose by confrontation and conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But because Singapore also makes solar panels, we also become collateral damage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This illustrates the danger of a full-blown trade war.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It has always been a cornerstone for peace and prosperity in our region.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: ASEAN unity enlarges our strategic and economic space, amplifies our voices on the international stage, and promotes an open and rules-based inclusive regional architecture.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The alternative, if we did not have ASEAN, is to become a bunch of vassal states operating on the principle of “might is right” and being an arena for proxy wars.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think Mr Low Thia Khiang also mentioned that yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, ASEAN is a cornerstone of our foreign policy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will work to strengthen the ASEAN-led regional architecture by working with our ASEAN member states and our dialogue partners.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our dialogue partners have proposed various regional initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For instance, I mentioned the B&R Initiative just now.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: More recently, Members may have heard the US, Japan and India talking about a Free and Open Indo-Pacific.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Without getting into the details, I would just like to share with Members how I view all these proposals.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First question: whatever the proposal is, whatever the label is, what does your proposal mean for ASEAN Centrality and unity?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In other words, will these initiatives keep ASEAN at the core of the regional architecture of Southeast Asia, or will they, wittingly or unwittingly, pull ASEAN apart and force us to choose sides?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second question: whatever the plan or initiative is, does it facilitate trade, investment, infrastructure and connectivity?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Clearly, an economic agenda, because ASEAN has got such growth potential in the next two to three decades.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Trade, investment, infrastructure and connectivity are a strategy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Our Chairmanship of ASEAN is an important opportunity for us, in our own small way, to make a positive contribution to a substantive and forward-looking agenda.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim mentioned her concern that, according to a survey, only 13% of Singaporeans expressed interest in ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But my own take is that I think we take it for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: After 50 years, we have taken it for granted that there is no war in Southeast Asia, that we transact with one another, have mutual interdependence, investments, trade.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: When we have disputes, we go to the international courts and we resolve disputes according to international laws.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Actually, if you look at the people level and you ask yourselves, tourism numbers – Singaporeans are great travellers and ASEAN is our immediate neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If you look at schools and you ask the schools about school trips, lots of trips.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On service learning, the Singapore International Foundation (SIF) volunteers, even when you look at both formal and informal volunteer groups and what our students and young people do in the more rural areas, even in Indochina.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: If you ask our businesses what their investments are across Malaysia and Indonesia, actually, if you do a proper catalogue, I think we are fully invested in ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is just that, I think, we take it for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We need to raise the flag of ASEAN more.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I am always intrigued that if you go to any ASEAN member state embassy, you will see us flying two flags ‒ our own national flag and our ASEAN flag.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But you do not often see the ASEAN flag in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, I take the Member's point that we do need to fly the flag more and to make our people appreciate how important ASEAN is to us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It expresses our hopes for ASEAN to meet future challenges, particularly to deal with emerging issues like digital disruption.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: After all, this is what we are also doing at the local level.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: How do we deal with the digital revolution?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, this is an opportunity for us to do more with our fellow ASEAN members.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We envisage it as a platform for ASEAN cities to share best practices, urban solutions, new technologies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But I think the most important thing is we are looking for interoperability, whether you are talking about e-payment systems, ASEAN single trade windows, facilitation of travel, facilitation of even the ASEAN self-certification regime in order to make it easier to export goods and services.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We want to do all these because, in fact, there is tremendous potential for intra-ASEAN trade.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Someone asked about the model ASEAN Extradition Treaty.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Negotiations are not over yet but making good progress.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: As ASEAN Chair, we will have to work hard to maximise our common ground and keep ASEAN united.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For instance, some Members ‒ I think it was Mr Louis Ng and Mr Christopher de Souza ‒ asked about the situation in Rakhine state.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Members are familiar that one of the founding principles of ASEAN is non-interference in domestic affairs.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But I would say this is a humanitarian disaster of the highest order.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, in our own quiet, behind-the-scenes way, we have to try to make a positive difference.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: ASEAN agreed to mobilise the ASEAN Coordinating Centre for Humanitarian Assistance (AHA) to deliver assistance to the affected communities in Myanmar and, when we delivered it, we insisted that it should be delivered without discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: All communities who need help should receive our help.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have also deployed an ASEAN Emergency Response and Assessment Team to assist in the humanitarian relief efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We had an ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Retreat last month.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Myanmar gave us a briefing, and we urged Myanmar to continue implementing the recommendations made by the Advisory Commission on Rakhine State which was led by former UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We encouraged the expeditious commencement of the voluntary return of the refugees.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But it has to be done in a safe, secure and dignified way, without undue delay.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Frankly, these are easier said than done when you consider what has already transpired on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have also emphasised that the responsibility for resolving this complex problem ultimately rests with Myanmar and the stakeholders within Myanmar.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore and ASEAN will continue to do our part by encouraging all partners to work towards a long-term and comprehensive political solution, and to create a conducive environment for affected communities to rebuild their lives.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There will always, from time to time, be an issue that tests our fundamental principles and our ability to make a positive contribution.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Another area that we are focused on right now is the ASEAN-China relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are reaching the end of our third year of our coordinatorship of the ASEAN-China Dialogue relationship.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In these three years, we have been able to strengthen the relationship despite the challenges, and it will culminate with 2018 designated as the "ASEAN-China Year of Innovation".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This year, 2018, marks the 15th Anniversary of the ASEAN-China Strategic Partnership, which we will commemorate with a statement on the ASEAN-China Strategic Partnership Vision 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This sets a roadmap for the future of the strategic partnership.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It will serve, we hope, to reinforce the rules-based regional order.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And as ASEAN-China coordinator, we will continue to be an honest broker.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will work closely with all sides to narrow the differences.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I cannot promise it will be delivered soon because of the complexities involved.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Ms Sun Xueling asked about economic integration and free trade.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Actually, free trade all over the world is unfairly blamed for the economic problems that, in fact, are the result of technological disruption.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We believe – and we have been discussing it during the Budget Debate – that the answer is not to build walls or to retreat from global competition.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But without getting into the fine print, the point is that AEC is an attempt to enable our companies to better access ASEAN's dynamic market of more than 600 million people where, as I have said earlier, 60% are below the age of 35 and there is enormous investment opportunity.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Fundamentally, I am glad that we do not argue about this in Singapore because, in Singapore, trade is our lifeline.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: No other state has a trading volume that is three-and-a-half times its GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is trade that allows our companies to expand beyond our small market and to create jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Although I have said that global consensus is eroding, the outlook is actually not so bleak.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We will continue to leave the door open for the US.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the meantime, we also hope to make substantive progress this year on RCEP.
